source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: LLM translates the problem into a logic program or constraint problem, a solver (Prolog, Prover9, Z3, python-constraint) runs it. This beat standard prompting and CoT on all five datasets for all three base models, with one exception noted in b02.
numbers: Table 2, GPT-4, Standard/CoT/Logic-LM: ProntoQA 77.4/98.8/83.2; ProofWriter 52.7/68.1/79.7; FOLIO 69.1/70.6/78.9; LogicalDeduction 71.3/75.3/87.6; AR-LSAT 33.3/35.1/43.0. Reported averages: +39.2% over standard and +18.4% over CoT with GPT-3.5; GPT-4 +24.98% and +10.44%.
quote: offloading the reasoning to symbolic solvers greatly improves faithfulness compared with pure language-based reasoning with CoT
limits: Wins are not uniform: on ProntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.8) beats Logic-LM (83.2). Fall back to CoT when the program does not run. Datasets are mostly synthetic except FOLIO and AR-LSAT.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for S2 Represent: write rules in a checkable form and let a solver do the deduction. Expect the largest gain when the problem needs search, case split or elimination rather than forward chaining.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM, boundary conditions: where CoT already works
finding: CoT already matches forward chaining, so the solver adds little on ProntoQA and ProofWriter-style tasks. Gains are biggest on tasks that need hypothesis, conditioning, recursion or elimination.
numbers: CoT gain over standard: ProntoQA +51.59%, ProofWriter +33.82%, but FOLIO +11.75%, LogicalDeduction +9.41%, AR-LSAT -3.2%. Logic-LM over CoT: FOLIO +21.85%, LogicalDeduction +45.67%, AR-LSAT +24.14% (GPT-3.5 averages as reported).
limits: Author explanation, not tested by an ablation.
agent_relevance: Route by task type: use the formal path for constraint or case-analysis problems; plain stepwise reasoning is enough for short forward chains.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM, translation bottleneck
finding: The hard part moves from reasoning to formalising. Programs on synthetic data nearly always run; on real exam-style text many do not. Self-refinement from solver error messages raises the executable rate but accuracy stalls after round 1-2.
numbers: GPT-4 executable rate without refinement: ProntoQA 100%, ProofWriter 99.0%, LogicalDeduction 100%, FOLIO 79.9%, AR-LSAT 32.6%. Self-refinement raised executable rate by 5.01 points on average (FOLIO GPT-4 79.9 to 85.8 per Table 3). ProofWriter depth test (300 per subset): Logic-LM beats CoT by 7.1, 5.0, 12.7, 20.0, 39.4 points at depths 0, 1, 2, 4, 5.
limits: Execution rate only measures syntax; execution accuracy is the semantic check. Error message feedback does not detect semantic mistranslation.
agent_relevance: Add a check on the translation itself (round trip back to words, test cases), not only on whether the program runs. Gain grows with proof depth, so use formal route for deep chains.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: neurosymbolic approach combining LMs with first-order logic provers
finding: LLM translates to first-order logic, Prover9 decides. Big gains for small and mid models, but for GPT-4 on FOLIO LINC did not beat CoT. A partial non-replication of the Logic-LM claim on the strongest model.
numbers: 10-way majority vote. FOLIO: StarCoder+ LINC 56.0 vs CoT 41.8; GPT-4 LINC 72.5 vs CoT 75.3 (McNemar p=0.58, not significant). ProofWriter balanced subset: GPT-3.5 96.4 and GPT-4 98.3 with LINC; StarCoder+ with LINC beat GPT-3.5 CoT by 38 points and GPT-4 CoT by 10 points.
limits: Scratchpad ablation (formulae written but solver removed) did not help, so the solver itself is the cause. Small sample per dataset; ProofWriter is synthetic.
agent_relevance: A formal route cannot be assumed to beat a strong model on natural text. Treat the formal check as a second opinion, and compare both.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC error analysis
finding: LINC and CoT fail in different ways, so they are complementary. LINC fails by lossy translation: missing implicit facts (such as Person(Harry)), merged predicates, syntax errors. It answers Uncertain too often.
numbers: GPT-4 FOLIO: LINC predicts Uncertain 57% vs CoT 41%. Precision when LINC says True or False 93% vs CoT 81%, but recall on True/False 60% vs 75%. Syntax errors in generated FOL: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4 (most common: same symbol with different arities). Overlap of mistakes: LINC with others 0.14-0.22 vs 0.52-0.56 among in-context methods.
limits: One dataset and model for the qualitative study.
agent_relevance: When the solver says True or False, trust it more than prose reasoning; when it says Uncertain, suspect a missing premise and add background facts before giving up. Run both routes and compare.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: satisfiability-aided language models using declarative prompting
finding: Declarative specification (constraints) sent to Z3 beats imperative program generation (PAL-style) because the LLM does not have to plan the solving order. New state of the art on LSAT and BoardgameQA over models trained on the full training sets.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy: GSM-SYS (hard subset) SatLM 69.4%, +23% over program-aided; with self-consistency 80.9%. GSM 84.8% with self-consistency. LSAT 30.9% to 37.4% SoTA; BoardgameQA 73.9% to 80.7%. Greedy COT on GSM-SYS 46.5, LSAT 23.5, BoardgameQA 60.7, ProofWriter 80.1.
limits: On plain GSM with greedy decoding SatLM lags the program-aided baseline; wins appear with self-consistency. Older Codex model.
agent_relevance: State the problem as constraints and facts (what is true), not as steps (what to do). Fits S2 Represent.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM, selective prediction
finding: The solver can say UNSAT (conflicting rules) or AMBIG (underdetermined), which a plain interpreter cannot. Abstaining on those cases raises accuracy of the answers that remain.
numbers: Selective accuracy on GSM-SYS: SatLM 77% vs program-aided 45%. SatLM answers fewer problems but is still better overall on GSM-SYS and CLUTRR.
limits: Coverage drops; fallback is needed.
agent_relevance: Use contradiction and underdetermination as signals: UNSAT means the translation is wrong or the premises conflict; AMBIG means a premise is missing. Feeds guardrails on unsupported answers.

source: Clark, Tafjord & Richardson (2020) Transformers as soft reasoners over language (RuleTakers)
finding: Rules and facts given in English (a Datalog-like fragment with negation as failure under closed-world assumption) can be reasoned over by a trained transformer, with high accuracy and transfer to deeper chains.
numbers: 99% accuracy on held-out synthetic test; 95%+ on depths unseen in training; 98% on crowd-paraphrased rules (ParaRules); 90%+ zero-shot on two hand-authored rulebases except one (66.6% on a harder one); model flags the critical sentences with F1 about 92 (P 98.7, R 86.9).
limits: Training was on synthetic data from the same generator. A model trained only to depth 0-1 scores below chance beyond depth 2, which shows reliance on distribution. RoBERTa on a rebuilt dataset dropped (83.3% vs 99.3%) when the generator changed.
agent_relevance: Pre-LLM baseline: soft reasoning looks perfect on synthetic rule worlds and breaks off distribution. This is why an external rule engine is attractive for S2.

source: Saparov & He (2023) Language models are greedy reasoners: a systematic formal analysis of chain-of-thought (PrOntoQA)
finding: Parsing the chain of thought into proofs shows single deduction steps are mostly valid. The failure is proof planning: when several valid steps are open, the model picks a misleading one and does not search.
numbers: 5-hop, fictional ontology: 93.2% of predicted proof steps strictly valid, 2.4% broadly valid, 5.9% invalid; 2.4% non-atomic although all examples were atomic. Most incorrect proofs contain misleading or invalid steps; some correct proofs do too. Accuracy is much higher with a true-world ontology than fictional or false ones.
limits: InstructGPT and GPT-3 family, not current models. ProntoQA is synthetic.
agent_relevance: Local inference is fine; search control is weak. A rule engine supplies the systematic search the model lacks.

source: Lyu et al. (2023) Faithful chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Two stages: LM writes a symbolic chain (Python, Datalog or PDDL), a deterministic solver answers. Beats CoT on 9 of 10 benchmarks and the chain is a true explanation of the answer. Datalog was used for relational inference (CLUTRR).
numbers: Relative gains with code-davinci-002 greedy: MWP +6.3% (up to 14.2%; GSM8K +14% on the hardest), Planning +3.4%, multi-hop QA +5.5%, Relational inference +21.4% (CLUTRR rises to 41.3% with self-consistency). With GPT-4: 95.0+ on 6 of the datasets, new few-shot state of the art on 7.
limits: No clear gain on StrategyQA and Sports (the difficulty there is knowledge retrieval, not reasoning). Gains shrink on easy datasets (0.3-2.4%). With self-consistency GSM8K gain falls from 9.0% to 2.6%.
agent_relevance: Gain is largest where the task is hard and relational. Where knowledge recall is the bottleneck, formalising does not help.

source: Yang, Ishay & Lee (2023) Coupling large language models with logic programming for robust and general reasoning from text
finding: LLM acts as few-shot semantic parser to atomic facts; answer set programs with reusable knowledge modules (event calculus, spatial rules) do the reasoning. Near perfect on bAbI, strong on StepGame noise, and exposed label errors in the benchmarks.
numbers: bAbI: text-davinci-003 few-shot 80.34%, CoT 86.18%, with ASP 99.99% (2 disagreements, both ambiguous questions). StepGame with noise (k=1..10): davinci-002+ASP 92.6, 89.9, 89.1, 93.8, 92.9, 91.6, 91.2, 90.4, 89.0, 88.3; GPT-3 CoT 25-61. About 10.7% of StepGame labels were wrong: of 108 disagreements in 1000 predictions, 107 were label errors.
limits: Hand-written domain knowledge modules; the weaker curie-001 parser gets 44.7-62.4 on StepGame, so the parser quality matters. 1000 test items per k (baselines on 100).
agent_relevance: Accuracy stays flat as chain length grows. Also a reminder to audit gold labels when a rule-based method disagrees with the dataset.

source: Borazjanizadeh & Piantadosi (2024/2025) Reliable reasoning beyond natural language
finding: LLM encodes the problem as Prolog (reasoning in text and logic code); retrying at higher temperature until the code executes. Near perfect on a new 55-problem non-linear reasoning set where text-only CoT collapses as variables depend on each other.
numbers: Navigate: all evaluated models above 98% with Prolog. NLR: GPT-4 up from as low as 8.3% to 100% on two of three categories. As variable interdependence rises from 1 to 4, text-only GPT-4 falls from 100% to 0% while Prolog stays stable. NLR has 55 problems (21 math word problems, 17 others); GSM8K also improves.
limits: Only 55 hand-made problems. Most execution failures were variable-name assignment errors, since Prolog variables are not mutable. The approach is evaluated mainly on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct test of Prolog as the target language. The benefit scales with how entangled the constraints are. Useful guideline: retry when the program does not run, take the first executable one.

source: Kirtania, Gupta & Radhakrishna (2024) Logic-LM++: multi-step refinement for symbolic formulations
finding: Refinement by solver error messages often fixes syntax but introduces wrong meaning (for example turning 'no young person teaches' into 'all young people teach'). Adding a pairwise comparison step that accepts a revision only if it is semantically better improves on Logic-LM.
numbers: On FOLIO, ProofWriter and AR-LSAT, average improvement of 18.5% over standard, 12.3% over CoT, 5% over Logic-LM. Execution accuracy up about 6% with GPT-4 and about 3% with GPT-3.5-turbo; execution rate gain under 1%.
limits: Gain over Logic-LM is modest (5%). Dependent on the LLM acting as a judge of its own edit.
agent_relevance: Name a rule: a repair must not just make the program run; check it against the original sentence. Matches the self-refinement stall in b03.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 CoT papers plus own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models: CoT helps mostly on math and symbolic tasks, and even there a symbolic solver beats it. With plan then execution split, plan plus tool solver (Z3 on FOLIO and ContextHub) beat plan plus CoT in most settings.
numbers: 20 datasets, 14 models, over 100 papers. Plans alone (plan plus direct answer) did not explain most of the CoT gain; execution tracking did.
quote: CoT appears to be a poor (but universal) approximation to such solvers.
limits: The FOLIO symbolic gain is less than in math; Z3 plan must parse (unparseable counted wrong or random).
agent_relevance: Independent, broad support for sending symbolic execution to a tool. Also supports skipping CoT on tasks without symbolic content.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Large language models meet symbolic provers for logical reasoning evaluation (ProverQA/ProverGen)
finding: A harder FOL benchmark built with a prover: strong models fall to near chance on the hard subset even with CoT, while older benchmarks look solved. Older sets overstate ability.
numbers: ProverQA (1,500 items, easy/medium/hard). CoT: GPT-4o 94.2/79.4/50.0; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 95.2/83.6/56.4; Mistral-Large 92.6/75.8/52.2; Llama3.1-8B 75.6/46.6/33.6. ProntoQA with CoT: GPT-4o 100.0, Claude 99.2. FOLIO CoT 72.1 and 80.7. Finetuned Llama3.1-8B on generated data improved in and out of distribution.
limits: Prompting only; no solver route tested in the table I read. Synthetic with LLM-written language.
agent_relevance: Test the formal route on hard, deep problems, not on ProntoQA where plain CoT is already at ceiling.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Can large language models understand DL-Lite ontologies? An empirical study
finding: Six tasks on description logic ontologies. LLMs read the formal syntax and the meaning of concepts and roles quite well, but fail on negative-inclusion (disjointness) transitivity and on ontologies with large ABoxes (many facts).
numbers: Precision, recall and F1 reported per task for GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, LLaMA3-8B variants; LLaMA3-8B improves clearly when given the syntax and explanation (WI/WIE) versus none (NI). Models gave wrong explanations for TBox NI transitivity rules.
limits: I did not extract exact F1 per cell. DL-Lite is a small fragment. Authors suggest a reversal-curse like effect for inverse roles.
agent_relevance: Do not ask the model to do DL-style subsumption in its head for long or fact-heavy knowledge bases; use a reasoner. The disjointness/negation weakness matches the LINC note on implicit facts.

source: Yang, Chen & Sattler (2026) Large language model for OWL proofs
finding: Reasoning models were tested on generating proofs over OWL (description logic) ontologies in three steps: Extraction, Simplification, Explanation, plus a task on logic completeness. Strong models are good on easy cases. Logical complexity, not formal versus natural language, drives errors. Noise and missing premises hurt most.
numbers: Some models exceed 90% on extraction while others are below 50%; weaker open model Qwen3-32B lags GPT-o4-mini by up to 33% in a weighted score. Accuracy fell up to 47% with large amounts of irrelevant axioms (justification to noise 1:20) and up to 38% when premises were missing. Table: Simp. Acc. 80.91 to 40.14 (-42.7%), Derivation Acc. 80.30 to 32.39 (-38.0%) in the harder condition.
limits: A few ontologies; the numbers are for the settings quoted, not an average over all models.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant facts degrade even formal reasoning by LLMs; filter the knowledge base to the relevant axioms before reasoning. Lacking premises is hard to detect.

source: Meng et al. (2025) OntoURL: benchmark for ontological understanding, reasoning and learning
finding: 15 tasks, 57,303 questions, 40 ontologies, 8 domains, 20 open models. Understanding tasks are easy, reasoning that uses logical operators (SWRL, description logic) is much harder, and learning (creating ontologies) is poor.
numbers: Largest models (Qwen2.5-72B, LLaMA3.3-70B) best. On the logic-operator reasoning tasks (R4 SWRL, R5 DL) scores are about 60-75% even for the best model. Few-shot helped: for example Qwen-72B up on some tasks (89.6% to 91.3% with 4-shot) while learning scores stayed low (BERTScore F1 about 20 or less).
limits: Open-weight models only, zero-shot default, generated questions.
agent_relevance: Logic with operators is a weak spot of unaided models. Reasoning in an ontology language needs the reasoner, not a prompt.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) appendix: FOLIO and ContextHub symbolic tasks
finding: Across 14 models, CoT versus direct answer on FOLIO (symbolic category) is clearly positive for large models; for ContextHub deductive level 2 the CoT gain is small or negative for many models.
numbers: FOLIO CoT vs direct: GPT-4o 79.8 vs 62.6; Llama 3.1 70b 70.9 vs 69.0; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 73.9 vs 68.5; Gemini 1.5 Pro 73.9 vs 74.4. ContextHub deductive L2: GPT-4o 54.5 vs 45.6; Gemini 1.5 Pro 57.3 vs 43.3; Mistral 7b 48.8 vs 55.1.
limits: I read which column is which only from the appendix table layout (CoT then direct); cell labels were not fully captured by the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Even with CoT, deduction with many hypothetical branches stays near 50-57%, leaving a gap for a solver route.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM, versus LINC (cross-paper comparison)
finding: Same idea (translate then solve), different outcomes with GPT-4 on FOLIO: Logic-LM reports 78.9 vs 70.6 for CoT; LINC reports 72.5 vs 75.3. The difference is probably the setup (fallback to CoT when the program fails, majority vote of 10, different prompts and data sample).
numbers: Logic-LM FOLIO GPT-4: Standard 69.1, CoT 70.6, Logic-LM 78.9, with CoT fallback for the 20.1% non-executable cases. LINC FOLIO GPT-4: CoT 75.3, LINC 72.5, no fallback (2% errors).
limits: My comparison, not a controlled one. Different subsets of FOLIO and different prompts.
agent_relevance: The combination (formal route, fall back to prose when it fails to run) may be the robust design; the formal route alone is not robustly better for strong models.

source: Saparov & He (2023) PrOntoQA: ontology type effect
finding: Model performs comparably on fictional and false ontologies (slightly worse for false) but much better with true ontology, so prior world knowledge props up the answer. Rules that fit the real world are partly retrieved, not reasoned.
numbers: Figure 4: accuracy in the true-ontology condition is clearly above fictional and false; exact values are in the figure and were not read from the text. Depth tested up to 5 hops.
limits: Exact accuracy values are only in the figure, so none are recorded here.
agent_relevance: Test the agent on made-up or counterfactual rules; a fact base with invented names removes the memory shortcut and tests real rule use.

source: Clark et al. (2020) RuleTakers, depth generalisation and shortcuts
finding: Models trained on shallow depth generalise partly; model trained to depth 3 reaches 95%+ on all depths; perturbation tests show the model is sensitive to the sentences that matter.
numbers: Removing a critical sentence flips the prediction from true to false 81% of the time (16,654 of 20,549); removing a non-critical sentence keeps the prediction in over 99% of cases. Depth-3 trained model 71.1% on Depth=3 per one training mix, and about 97.6% on depth 5 per another (as extracted).
limits: Some numbers in my extraction are partial; the two depth figures come from different training mixes.
agent_relevance: Good test for rule use: delete one needed premise and see whether the answer flips, then delete a distractor and see whether it stays.

source: Yang et al. (2023) GPT-3+ASP: parser dependence
finding: The result depends on the LLM being a good parser. A weaker model gives a large drop even when the logic program is perfect.
numbers: StepGame k=10: curie-001+ASP 54.1% vs davinci-002+ASP 88.3%; k=1: 44.7 vs 92.6. Few-shot (d3) 55.0 at k=1 and 32.0 at k=5.
limits: GPT-3 era models; 100 test items for the GPT-3 baselines.
agent_relevance: The scaffold's gain is capped by how well the agent turns text into facts. Spend effort on the extraction step and check extracted facts.

source: Borazjanizadeh & Piantadosi (2025) multiple-try rule
finding: Retrying until the Prolog code runs (higher temperature each time, up to a preset maximum) and using the first executable answer, instead of majority vote, was their inference rule. They state that failures come mostly from variable naming under immutability.
numbers: No numeric ablation of retries was read from the text.
limits: The exact retry count and ablation are not in the sections I read.
agent_relevance: Cheap and simple: a hard validity filter (program must run) is a different check from voting, and fits guardrails on checkable output.

source: Wang et al. (2024) DL-Lite, ABox size
finding: As the number of facts grows, models struggle to hold them all in a prompt; instance checking works for small ABoxes and degrades when ABoxes are large. Authors recommend more faithful knowledge engineering tools.
numbers: Instance checking tested at different ABox sizes with GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, LLaMA3-8B; exact F1 per size not recorded here.
limits: Numbers not extracted from the tables.
agent_relevance: Keep fact sets small in context; store the rest in a queryable base and fetch what is needed.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM, log-likelihood and fluency
finding: Where SatLM beats program-aided models, its generated outputs also have higher model likelihood, which suggests declarative text is closer to the problem wording and so easier for the LLM to write.
numbers: Higher total and normalised log likelihood on GSM-SYS and CLUTRR where SatLM wins (Table 4).
limits: Correlational.
agent_relevance: Supports writing rules close to the original words rather than as a procedure.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM ablation: self-refinement rounds on FOLIO
finding: Rounds of self-refinement from solver error text: executable rate keeps rising but accuracy plateaus.
numbers: FOLIO accuracy goes 66.7 to 79.4 to 85.3 style steps in the executable rate over rounds 0-3 (as read in the figure text: 66.7%, 79.9%, 79.4%, 85.3%); accuracy stagnates after the first rounds.
limits: The figure text was garbled by extraction, so the pairing of numbers with rounds is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Cap repair at one or two rounds; later rounds only fix syntax.
